citations.quote: This paper presents the first efforts of the development of an open-source initiative for the modeling of CubeSats starting from the PD studies. It discusses the formalization of a CubeSat Systems Modelling Language (SysML) general model, enhanced through the use of a newly-generated set of Unified Modelling Language (UML) stereotypes.

The application of UML stereotypes within a SysML model tailored ad-hoc for CubeSat PD is shown to offer several advantages, including enhanced data characterization, reusability, and system optimization. The formalization offers a centralized, adaptable data source that integrates seamlessly with simulation tools, improving design accuracy and efficiency.

This formalization enables the CubeSat model to serve as the central source of truth for data management across all phases of the PD phase. This integrative approach streamlines communication, reduces inconsistencies, and enhances traceability of design decisions across the various stages of development.
This paper builds on the foundation established in [9] and delves into the principal design choices underlying the proposed formalization.

The work presented in [9], originated by a Master's Thesis work [11] conducted in collaboration between Polytechnic University of Turin (Turin, IT) and ISAE-Supaero (Toulouse, FR), constitutes the backbone of this work.
The model is intended to serve as a central data reference throughout all stages of the Preliminary Design (PD) phase, functioning as the primary design interface and source of truth for data.

Another key result is the generalization of Operating Modes (OMs) for CubeSats by identifying common attributes and transition criteria among different Low Earth Orbit (LEO) CubeSat Concepts of Operations (ConOps's). This allows mission scenarios to be defined by modifying OM attributes, regardless of the data format.

A proof of concept is demonstrated using the SysML model of the "The White Compass (TWC)" theoretical mission, integrated with the Nanostar Software Suite (NSS) [12, 13] analysis tools through a dedicated parser, successfully producing power and data budgets $ ^{1} $ .

citations.quote: Two main requirements have been imposed for the formalization presented in [9]: the exclusive use of open-source tools, following the principle of Open Science, and the use of a single model, inclusive of all mission parameters to facilitate the PD phase of a CubeSat without the need to refer to an external database.

The question to be answered by the proposed formalization was then whether it was possible to use MBSE as a frontend for the entire design cycle of a CubeSat, with the exclusive use of open-source tools.

Through the introduction of several stereotypes, it becomes possible to specialize the SysML Block element into System, Component, Orbit, GroundStation or OperatingMode new elements, each one of them inheriting a standardized set of attributes for their characterization.

By introducing such a stereotype, the designer can create any desired Orbit element by adding the appropriate values to the pre-defined set of attributes that the element will inherit (i.e., in this instance, the orbital parameters). More generally, once the stereotypes are incorporated into the model, they can be reused for various designs by simply adjusting the input data.
Once the stereotypes are integrated into the model, they can be reused across multiple designs without needing to recreate the structure or redefine attributes.
Designers only need to update the specific data points, such as mass or power consumption, to reflect changes in the design or mission requirements.

Moreover, the parser - by knowing in advance the set of stereotypes and therefore the attributes introduced with them - automatically extracts the relevant data from the elements of the SysML model with a specific stereotype applied and converts them into a software-readable format.
This eliminates the need for manual data entry on each simulation tool, reducing the possibility of human error and significantly speeding up the design process.

For example, if a simulation tool determines an optimized power consumption profile, this data can be updated in the model without manual intervention. This automated update capability supports an agile and responsive design process, where the model is contin-

With the same principles used for data extraction, the use of stereotypes in the formalization also supports the generation of dependency graphs as the one shown in Fig. 6, which visually depict the relationships between different system components and how changes in one parameter (e.g., mass or power consumption) affect other parts of the system.

For example, increasing the power consumption of a system may require adjustments to the power budget, battery capacity, or solar array specifications. By visualizing these dependencies, designers can make more informed decisions and optimize system performance while managing trade-offs between competing design constraints.

With the standardized data structure provided by stereotypes, different teams (e.g., power systems, communications, thermal management) can work concurrently on the same model, ensuring that their contributions are integrated seamlessly.

The current framework was developed using Gaphor [27], an open-source modeling tool, and the parser designed for data extraction is tailored specifically to this tool. This creates limitations in terms of interoperability with other SysML tools, such as Papyrus [28] or Capella [29], which may store or structure their model files differently. As a result, the parser would require significant modification to be compatible with other tools, making the framework less flexible for users who prefer or are required to use different SysML platforms.

A temporary limitation is that the framework is focused solely on LEO CubeSat missions at the time being. Making it less suitable for complex missions involving non-nominal conditions, such as Early Orbit Phase (EOP) or off-nominal scenarios (e.g., detumbling or calibration). Customization for specialized missions can be time-consuming, especially when new stereotypes are required for novel subsystems, increasing the complexity of the model.

The success of the approach heavily depends on the accuracy of the initial SysML model. Any inaccuracies or omissions can propagate through the system, leading to flawed simulations or incorrect system budgets. This necessitates thorough validation of the model, increasing the workload in the design phase.

For larger teams, inconsistent application of stereotypes can cause data fragmentation, leading to synchronization issues across subsystems and complicating system-wide analyses. Strict version control and collaboration protocols would be necessary but could increase management overhead.
This continuous maintenance could become burdensome, especially for teams that lack the resources or expertise to make these updates in a timely manner.

If the parser does not function as expected, the data flow between the SysML model and simulation tools may be disrupted, which could slow down the design process or lead to delays in generating necessary outputs like system budgets.

To maximize the benefits of the formalization while mitigating its drawbacks, future development should focus on increasing tool compatibility, expanding the scope for complex missions, and simplifying customization processes.

The system's capability to manage both qualitative and quantitative data within a unified model is an essential advancement for systems development, where efficient resource management (power, mass, etc.) is critical.
Future work can expand the scope of the proposed formalization to address more complex and non-standard CubeSat missions.
The source code and documentation are publicly available at https://gitlab.isae-supaero.fr/preliminary-design/mbse-cubesat-sysml, under GPLv3 license.

citations.quote: By knowing in advance the relationship between the data included within the stereotypes (e.g., system's power consumption and OMs overall power consumption), and by reading in the SysML the connections between the elements with specific stereotypes applied (e.g., composite associations between components and main systems), the data extraction process can automatically generate these graphs, which are particularly valuable for conducting trade-off studies during the PD phase.
Moreover, the formalization's ability to automate the extraction of data through a dedicated parser ensures that the data flow remains consistent across different tools and stages of design.

Another potential application is the use of these stereotypes in Multi-Disciplinary Optimization (MDO) environments, where the CubeSat system must be optimized across various domains (thermal, structural, electrical, etc.).
